meta.name: Microsoft Security Operations Analyst (SC-200)
meta.notes: Initial pack: 10 questions covering Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Microsoft Sentinel, threat hunting, and incident response. | 2026-05-23 keyword-balance pass

questions.question: A SOC running Microsoft Defender for Endpoint wants confirmed malicious files on developer workstations to be remediated automatically, but actions on production servers must wait for an analyst's approval. Which configuration achieves this with the least administrative effort?
options: Set the global tenant automation level to Full and exclude all server device names from automated investigation runs in the Defender for Endpoint settings
Create two device groups and set workstations to Full automatic remediation while servers require analyst approval for any remediation action taken

Disable automated investigation tenant-wide and have analysts review and approve every remediation action manually — disabling automation removes the Full automatic remediation benefit for workstations and forces analysts to approve every alert rather than only server analyst-approval cases
Tag developer workstations as Tier 1 and add an indicator rule that blocks automated remediation against server FQDNs across the entire tenant scope
questions.explanation: Device groups in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint scope the automated investigation and remediation (AIR) level independently per group. Workstations set to Full let MDE auto-remediate confirmed threats, while a Semi-level on servers (require approval for any remediation) holds actions pending analyst review. A single tenant-wide automation level cannot differ per device. Disabling AIR removes the value of the platform. Indicator rules block IOCs — they do not gate AIR behavior on a device subset.

questions.question: Microsoft Defender for Identity raises a 'Suspected DCSync attack' alert pointing at a service account used by an authorized vulnerability scanner that legitimately replicates directory data. Which response prevents recurring false positives while preserving detection against unknown principals?
options: Close the alert as a false positive and add the scanner service account to the Honeytoken exclusion list — Honeytoken exclusions apply to decoy credentials, not to legitimate service accounts suspected of performing benign DCSync-like replication operations
Close the alert as a true positive benign and add the scanner account as a sensitive account so all of its activity gets more closely monitored
Close the alert as a false positive and exclude the scanner service account from the Suspected DCSync attack detection in the alert exclusion settings
Disable the Suspected DCSync attack detection rule across the tenant and rely on Microsoft Sentinel KQL hunting queries against the SecurityEvent table for future detections
questions.explanation: Defender for Identity supports per-detection exclusions; excluding the scanner from the Suspected DCSync attack detection silences the false positive while keeping the detector active for any other principal. Honeytoken accounts are decoys that should never authenticate, so adding a real working account would generate noise on every legitimate use. Sensitive accounts heighten alerting rather than suppress it. Disabling the detection globally loses real detections.

questions.question: Users keep receiving phishing emails that link to freshly registered domains and slip past Exchange Online Protection. The tenant has Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2. Which feature, configured correctly, rewrites links in inbound mail and scans the destination at time of click?
options: Safe Attachments policy applied to all recipients with Dynamic Delivery enabled so the body of the message arrives while attachments are detonated
Anti-phishing policy with mailbox intelligence-based impersonation protection enabled on all users to block lookalike sender domains automatically
Safe Links policy applied to recipient mailboxes with URL rewriting and the Track user clicks option both enabled across the inbound mail flow

Exchange mail flow rule that automatically strips every HTML hyperlink from inbound email — stripping all links breaks legitimate email functionality; Safe Links rewrites URLs so they pass through inspection when clicked rather than removing the links before delivery
questions.explanation: Safe Links rewrites URLs in inbound mail and performs reputation and detonation checks at click time, catching domains weaponized after delivery. Safe Attachments only inspects file payloads. Mailbox intelligence guards against spoofed-sender impersonation, not URL reputation on arbitrary domains. Stripping all hyperlinks at the transport layer breaks legitimate mail and is not the supported control here.

questions.question: A team must prevent users on unmanaged devices from downloading files from SharePoint Online while still allowing browser-based read access. Which combination of Microsoft controls delivers exactly this requirement?
options: An Intune app protection policy on the SharePoint mobile app that prevents save-as operations to non-corporate storage from any unmanaged device platform
A SharePoint Online unmanaged-devices policy that requires a managed device plus Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels that mark these files as confidential
An Entra Conditional Access policy that grants access only after MFA plus a Defender for Cloud Apps access policy that blocks the user session entirely
An Entra Conditional Access policy that routes the session through Defender for Cloud Apps plus a session policy that blocks downloads of sensitive files
questions.explanation: Conditional Access App Control routes the session through Defender for Cloud Apps' reverse proxy; a session policy can block downloads of files matching label, classification, or content-inspection criteria while keeping read in the browser. The unmanaged-devices policy in SharePoint blocks access (or limits to view-only without download) at a coarser level and is not paired with sensitivity-aware enforcement. An access policy makes a binary allow/block decision and cannot enforce per-action controls. Intune app protection covers mobile apps, not browser SharePoint.

questions.question: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raises a High user-risk score on an account whose credentials were observed in a leaked credential dump. Which automated response best matches Microsoft's recommended pattern for high user risk?
options: A Conditional Access policy that requires multifactor authentication on every sign-in for all users, regardless of their high user risk score — blanket MFA on every sign-in does not differentiate high-risk users or require them to reset their password to clear the risk signal
A Conditional Access policy that requires a secure password change when user risk is High and that combines the requirement with enforced MFA on the account
An Intune device compliance rule that wipes the corporate workload from the user's device after three consecutive risky sign-ins have been recorded by Entra
A Sentinel playbook that disables the affected user account in Active Directory the very first time any user-risk signal is raised in the Entra ID Protection portal
questions.explanation: User risk represents the probability that an identity itself is compromised (e.g., leaked credentials). Microsoft's recommended response is a secure password change combined with MFA, replacing the leaked secret and confirming presence. MFA alone (sign-in risk) does not rotate the leaked password. Wiping the device addresses an endpoint, not an identity. Disabling on any signal is over-broad, ignores remediation paths, and breaks self-service MFA recovery flows.

questions.question: An analyst opens an incident in the Microsoft Defender portal that correlates alerts from Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365, and Defender for Identity. They want a single KQL query joining device, email, and identity telemetry. Which table set is correct?
options: AlertEvidence and AlertInfo alone, since advanced hunting inside the Defender portal exposes only those two consolidated alert-level tables to authorized hunters
SecurityEvent, OfficeActivity, and SigninLogs in the Microsoft Sentinel workspace tables exposed through the Log Analytics query interface for that workspace
WindowsEvent, AzureActivity, and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs in the same Log Analytics workspace bound to the Defender portal connector for hunting
DeviceProcessEvents, EmailEvents, and IdentityLogonEvents in the Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema accessed through the unified Defender portal
questions.explanation: The Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema exposes Device*, Email*, Identity*, App*, Cloud*, and Alert* tables and joins them across product telemetry inside the Defender portal. Sentinel-side tables (SecurityEvent, SigninLogs, OfficeActivity) live in Log Analytics and are queried from Sentinel, not from the Defender portal hunting page. AlertEvidence/AlertInfo exist but are a small subset; raw activity tables sit alongside them.

questions.question: A multicloud team needs Microsoft Defender for Cloud to surface an attack path showing how an internet-facing AWS EC2 instance could pivot to a sensitive Azure SQL database. Which prerequisite must be satisfied for Cloud Security Explorer to render this path?
options: Enable the Foundational CSPM (free) plan in Defender for Cloud, since attack paths require only basic posture data — attack-path analysis and cloud security graph features are only available in the paid Defender CSPM plan and require connectors to the database services
Enable the Defender CSPM (paid) plan on both the Azure subscription containing the SQL database and on the AWS connector account that contains the EC2 instance
Deploy the Azure Monitor Agent on the EC2 instance and stream Linux syslog into the Defender for Cloud workspace so that cross-cloud telemetry can be correlated
Onboard the AWS account through the Microsoft Sentinel AWS data connector and rely on Sentinel analytics rules to map the cross-cloud attack path for the SOC team
questions.explanation: Cloud Security Explorer and attack path analysis are features of the paid Defender CSPM plan and require it enabled on each environment whose resources participate in the path — in this scenario both the Azure subscription and the AWS connector account. Foundational CSPM only gives free recommendations and secure score, not attack-path graphs. Agents are not required; Defender CSPM uses agentless scanning. Sentinel ingests logs but does not build the cross-cloud graph that powers attack-path analysis.

questions.question: A team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to detect when a critical Azure Storage account starts receiving an unusual surge of access from a previously unseen IP, suggesting potential data exfiltration. Which workload protection plan must be enabled on the storage account's subscription?
options: Microsoft Defender for Key Vault, since any successful exfiltration of storage data would require the attacker to access the key vault to decrypt — Defender for Key Vault monitors key vault access anomalies, not anomalous access patterns to the storage account itself
Microsoft Defender for Resource Manager, which inspects management-plane API calls against the storage account's role assignments and Azure Policy definitions
Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2, since every storage account exposes an underlying virtual machine that hosts the blob, queue, and table service endpoints
Microsoft Defender for Storage, which baselines normal access patterns and alerts on anomalous behavior such as unfamiliar geographic source IPs or odd request bursts
questions.explanation: Defender for Storage monitors data-plane operations on storage accounts and generates alerts for anomalous access, suspicious IPs, malware uploads, and exposure events. Defender for Resource Manager observes control-plane (ARM) operations, not data-plane patterns. Storage accounts are PaaS and do not expose a customer-managed VM. Defender for Key Vault watches key operations, which is unrelated to whether storage uses customer-managed keys at all.

questions.question: A Microsoft Sentinel analyst needs a scheduled analytics rule that opens an incident when a single user fails sign-in to Microsoft Entra ID more than 50 times within any 10-minute window from any source IP. Which KQL pattern matches the requirement?
options: SigninLogs | where ResultType != 0 | summarize FailedCount = count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where FailedCount > 50
SigninLogs | where ResultType == 0 | summarize SuccessCount = dcount(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName | where SuccessCount > 50 in any window observed
AuditLogs | where Result == "failure" | summarize Bursts = count() by InitiatedBy_user_userPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where Bursts > 50
SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | summarize FailedCount = count() by Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where FailedCount > 50 across windows
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID sign-in failures land in SigninLogs with a non-zero ResultType. Binning by 10 minutes and thresholding above 50 implements the requirement directly. Option B counts successful sign-ins, not failures, and uses dcount of IPs. AuditLogs holds directory-change events, not authentication outcomes, and uses a 1-hour window. SecurityEvent / 4625 captures on-prem Windows logon failures collected by the MMA or AMA agent, not Entra ID cloud sign-ins.

questions.question: A Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule fires hundreds of low-severity incidents per day. The SOC wants every newly created incident from that rule whose tactic is Discovery and whose status is New closed automatically, without writing custom code. Which Sentinel feature delivers this?
options: An automation rule triggered on incident creation with conditions on the rule name and the Discovery tactic and an action that changes the status of the incident to Closed

A Logic Apps playbook triggered on every newly created incident that calls the Microsoft Sentinel API to check the rule name, tactic, and status, then sets matching incidents to closed — a Logic Apps playbook can close incidents but cannot evaluate the incident's rule name or discovery tactic as native conditions the way automation rules can
A Microsoft Sentinel watchlist of suppressed rule names that the scheduled analytics rule consults using lookup() before it is allowed to generate any new incident at runtime
An incident triage workbook that visualizes the noisy analytics rule and lets analysts mass-close matching incidents through an embedded custom JavaScript visualization control
questions.explanation: Automation rules in Microsoft Sentinel run on incident creation or update with simple condition-and-action logic and can close incidents directly — no code required. Playbooks (Logic Apps) are powerful but unnecessary for a built-in action, and deleting incidents loses audit trail. Watchlists store reference data; they cannot suppress rule output. Workbooks are read-only dashboards, not enforcement tools.
